posts.name: Christopher
posts.cooked:
I ran several SC RPG demos at Con in the Castle a couple weeks before Gen Con. In one of those demos, I had 4 players. One was a very experienced RPG player, but had never heard of anything from Sentinel Comics. One had never played RPGs, but played Sentinels of the Multiverse with some regularity. And the remaining two had never played any RPGs and were not familiar with Sentinel Comics, but had heard that the demo I was running was fun and decided, "Why not?"

That may have been the most fun game I ran that weekend. I gave everyone a brief overview of each of the characters and my usual run down on the rules. The 3 brand new RPGers did not need any more information than the experienced RPGer. The game is REALLY easy to pick up. Everyone got the characters quickly. But, then, that's the beauty of the Freedom Five. Sure, they have their depth and complexities, but they can be a straight-forward, easy to understand team. Each of the players naturally gravitated to certain characters, and soon, Bunker, The Wraith, Absolute Zero, and Unity made their way to the Wagner Space Center in downtown Megalopolis to attend the unveiling of the teleportation portal.

The game was a huge success. I was pleased that the experienced RPGer didn't overpower the other three. And it wasn't because he was showing restraint. The mechanics of the game make it so the game rewards imagination more than it does deep familiarity with rulesets. And the one player who knew the Sentinel Comics world wasn't nay-saying the other players. Everyone played their characters perfectly. Hell, the Bunker character did a BUNCH of things as Tyler Vance out of the armor, making me come up with stats for that on the fly. (Which, in turn, made me realize Lieutenant Vance will need some un-armored stats in the core game. Hooray! Successful playtesting!)

Anyway, I just wanted to share that success story, because that game made me realize what a fantastic system Cam, Dave, and Phil have come up with. I am honored to be working with them.

Even when Cam does this.

I’m definitely in agreement here. There are more than enough “generic” game systems out there–I’d much rather have a game that focuses specifically on a specific genre or sub-genre than a game system that acts as a “catch-all” for any genre out there.

Honestly? That may be my biggest worry in terms of the SCRPG. Superhero comics are a huge umbrella, wherein lurk everything from hard sci-fi to investigative crime drama to grindhouse horror to geopolitical spy games to cosmic psychedelia.

There are a ton of superhero games out there already that cover “superhero comics”: Mutants and Masterminds, Champion/HERO, Heroes Unlimited, and a ton more less-well-known systems. The problem with most of these is exactly that: they try to do everything and end up taking a middle-of-the-road approach that doesn’t do any justice to the specific genre tropes of those comics within the umbrella. They might be good systems, but they’re rarely built with any of those smaller approaches in mind. They choose breadth over depth.

I wrote Cold Steel Wardens: Roleplaying in the Iron Age of Comics for the opposite approach. I wanted to create a game where being the World’s Greatest Detective mattered just as much as your combat ability, where a ‘mask’ who wasn’t careful would fall in a hail of bullets, and where moral dilemma had a tangible impact on the game on a regular basis. As such, I built in rules to emphasize these elements. I chose depth over breadth. I’m well aware that my game may not appeal to some people. That’s fine–people enjoy different things. However, my time running full tables on the convention circuit tells me that there’s quite a bit of interest in this type of supers-gaming. It’s not for everyone, but it’s definitely perfect for some people.

I asked the question up above regarding specific sub-genres–which was answered well, if with the vagueness that comes with discussing an unreleased game–for specifically that reason. From what I’ve seen thusfar, the SCRPG seems more intent on focusing on the tropes of the comics themselves (pages and panels, dramatic challenge scenes, and the like) coupled with the tropes specific to the SotM universe.

In approach, this reminds me most of Cartoon Action Hour–a game meant to emulate 80s-era animation. CAH does this by including items in their rules-set that replicate 80s cartoons: characters can’t curse, heroes with a Sword of Power never actually use it to slash or stab anyone, and there are actual rules for commercial breaks. However, CAH has a series of “dials” in their GMing section that really helps you articulate the differences between, say, a game meant to ape Masters of the Universe from a game meant to resemble Jem and the Holograms.

I’m really hoping that the SCRPG has those sorts of ‘dials’ to help with adjusting the scale of an SCRPG game. Darkwatch patrolling the streets of Rook City should feel different than the Freedom Five fighting robots on Wagner Mars Base, which should feel different from Captain Cosmic patrolling the Enclave of the Endlings. To me, the more that’s built into the system to articulate those differences, the better the game will be.

Pydro:

Would you say that it is a Sentinels RPG or a super hero RPG that takes place in the Sentinels setting?

Christopher:

That is a fascinating question!

What would you say is the difference, in your mind?

You have two groups sitting down to play the same RPG system. Both groups are very familiar with SotM, and neither group is told the name of the RPG.

Group A Plays: TheChattyDM:

As Grand Warlord Voss planned to invade Wagner Mars Base, he sent Gene Bound humans to infiltrate the Wagner Space Centre in the outskirts of Megalopolis. He needed them to create a diversion during the unveiling of an experimental wormhole portal so they could find and recuperate the codes to deactivate the base' Self-Destruct sequence.

The heroes all attended the unveiling in various roles the players chose to play. For instance, in almost all cases, Tachyon played a role as a scientist on the project. Wraith often attended as Maya Montgomery, among the VIPs.

The portal exploded upon activation (sabotage!) and a LOT of things went wrong at the same time, giving each character more than one problem to act upon. So it was what I call a "complex scene" where combat and non combat threats had to be dealt with before the scene went critical (i.e. went passed RED) and everyone got sucked in the collapsing portal.

Then, all heroes were sent to Mars to kick out Voss who had launched his assault of the base. This was a more straightforward combat encounter using both a supervillain, many minions and the environment itself (who also as a turn, rolls dice and has various kickers that also double as costs for when thinmgs invariably go wrong).

Group B Plays: Bizzaro TheChattyDM:

As Emperor Tengu planned to invade Juxton Moon Base, he sent brainwashed humans to infiltrate the Juxton Space Centre in the outskirts of Bovil City. He needed them to create a diversion during the unveiling of an experimental wormhole portal so they could find and recuperate the codes to deactivate the base's Self-Destruct sequence.

The heroes all attended the unveiling in various roles the players chose to play. For instance, in almost all cases, Dr. Pluto played a role as a scientist on the project. Plasma often attended as Jill Hawthorne, among the VIPs.

The portal exploded upon activation (sabotage!) and a LOT of things went wrong at the same time, giving each character more than one problem to act upon. So it was what I call a "complex scene" where combat and non combat threats had to be dealt with before the scene went critical (i.e. went passed RED) and everyone got sucked in the collapsing portal.

Then, all heroes were sent to the Moon to kick out Emperor Tengu who had launched his assault of the base. This was a more straightforward combat encounter using both a supervillain, many minions and the environment itself (who also as a turn, rolls dice and has various kickers that also double as costs for when things invariably go wrong).

I think it is safe to assume that after the session, Group A would say "We just played an great Sentinels RPG!"

However, would Group B say the same thing, or would they say, "We just played a great super-hero RPG!"

posts.name: Pydro
posts.cooked:
It can be done by relying on the themes of the world. By haivng similar struggles, confrontations, and story rules, they can transcend the specific mechanic limitations of each medium. For example, you can easily have a Star Wars game withtout any of the main characters, or any character you have heard of by maintaining the theme. The struggle between the light side and the dark side. Or, you can easily have different types of Cthulu games by having a major dark presence, issues of insanity, etc. You can take these main ideas and themes and plug them into different mechanics.

If the only thing that makes this a Sentinels RPG is the name of the specific characters, then it is more of a super-hero RPG with a Sentinals setting, not a Sentinels RPG. There is nothing inherent in the game that makes it "Sentinels".

That being said, it would be an interesting conversation as to what makes Sentinels, Sentinels. The reliance on super-hero sterotypes and homages can hinder the uniqueness of the world, which could be why so much of the info we have been giving seems to point to a super-hero RPG with Sentinels setting. It is hard to distinguish what makes Sentinels unique.

This was one of the reason why I brought up the idea of time travel. The simple idea that nothing that happens is permanent seems to be a big part of the overall theme, at least for certain characters. Knowing that things can be changed, albeit with difficulty, adds a certain unique feel to the game. Add to that that there are specific points in time that must happen, and you have a possible unique theme for Sentinels. I am not saying that this is THE Sentinels theme, but it is one that seems to motivate a lot of actions.

aidanhurst:

Thank you Phil for all the information you've given us. Two questions if I may;

  1. Can you talk a little bit more about how experience will work?

  2. What sort of timeline are you looking at for the beta/getting more playtesters involved and are there any open slots for playtesters?

It's been a pleasure!

  1. As of now (subject to change), experience represents the number of adventures your character has been in since you started playing with it. Each adventure gives you "an issue" in a comic book collection.  During play, you score "spotlight moments", moments where your hero shines through great success, great failures or just plain weird events. There are mechanics that cover how to get those moments.

At the end of an adventure (that can last from one to a few sessions)  all players tally up thier spotlight moments. The character(s) with the most are featured as the main character(s) of that particular issue. And the group names the issue appropriately. (ex: Legacy #52: Peril on Mars) or (Legacy and Unity Special #2: Portal Trouble in Idaho). All other players are considered secondary characters in that issue.

Players mark both types of issues on their character sheets: Spotlight ones and ordinary issues where they were secondary characters. There are mechanics to make it harder for players to get consecutive spotlight issues. 

So XPs are like a comic book collection that tells of your previous adventure.

You tap into them in two ways:

Callbacks: Once per spotlight issue per adventure, you can callback to a previous adventure where your hero did something that would help you in a particular situation. Doing so either counts as minor cost to offset a minor failure, or allows you to Max out one die of your pool after a roll.

Trade Paperbacks: Once you get 6 issues in your collection, regardless if they are spotlight or not, you trade them away and your character "levels up" and gets a dice size increase on a power/quality and other options we're working on. 

I'm real excited about these (as I came up with a few of the ideas behind them, refined by Cam and Dave. amazing designers that they are.)

  1. I can't answer that, because I don't know. I know people can't wait to playtest this, but it's not entirely in our control and much of our energy is spent on designing the bits that are still missing.

Doing so either counts as minor cost to offset a minor failure, or allows you to Max out one die of your pool after a roll.Trade Paperbacks: Once you get 6 issues in your collection, regardless if they are spotlight or not, you trade them away and your character "levels up" and gets a dice size increase on a power/quality and other options we're working on. I'm real excited about these (as I came up with a few of the ideas behind them, refined by Cam and Dave. amazing designers that they are.)

This seems very reminiscent of the classic Deadlands methodology of XP, wherein you could spend Fate Chips for rerolls and to activate in-game benefits, but those same Fate Chips acted as your character's personal XP.  

It's worth noting, I think, that a lot of games have moved away from this, based on the tendency for players to be reticent to "burn their experience points" for a one-time bonus.  The current edition of Deadlands–and Savage Worlds in general–don't use this method; experience and Fate Chips are kept entirely separate.

While I tend to like games that include some form of meta-currency–Bennies, Fate points, Hero points, Vigilance dice, etc.–I don't think tying that currency to a character's advancement is a great idea…

  1. I may only have myself(GM) and two other players, is it reasonable to run a two player adventure or like the card game its designed for 3+ heroes? Or 2 players is possible but I'll have to modify the rules/senarios?

I'm not Phil, but:

Most narrative-focused games work even for one player. Hell, even crunchy games can, but you have to supplement the character (in D&D, this would be things like lots of health potions). My ideal game is for 3-4 players at a table. Less isn't bad, but more tends to be. The less players you have, the main problem ends up being those players having to share a lot of burden for pushing their story. With more players, you can hope for a little distribution of interest in that way. But if your players are really interested in the subject and the game, less players might be better and let you tell more intimate, richer stories.

I ran an MHR game for two players for a while. It went very well. I would be shocked if this did not work just as well.
